Teleoperation is the default way to collect robot demonstrations, and it is expensive for two reasons: the robot and the operator are occupied for every episode, and every new task restarts from zero. A new work asks a blunt question — can a coding agent take over the teleoperator's job?

**PyRUA-DataFarm**, posted to arXiv on 3 November, says yes, with a caveat worth reading carefully.

## How It Works

The agent receives a data request and **one calibration episode** of the robot in the target scene. It then rebuilds the entire task in simulation: it writes the scene, an expert controller, and a success judge. From there the pipeline runs itself. The simulator supplies **exact actions**, and a video model conditioned on the real images renders each rollout as photographic video — generating **all camera views together consistently**, which is the part that makes the output usable rather than merely plausible. What comes out is "real-ready" data: synchronized camera views labeled with the robot's actions, on which a policy can be trained directly and deployed on the physical robot.

Independent judges certify both the expert and every rendered episode before admission, so bad rollouts are filtered rather than silently trained on.

## The Numbers

On **five real-robot tasks**, policies trained only on farm data matched policies trained on the same number of teleoperated episodes: **93 versus 84 successes in 100 trials**. The gap widens under distribution shift — with an **unseen tablecloth and coloured light**, the farm-trained policies held **87 successes while the teleoperation-trained policies fell to 46**.

The cost story is the headline:

- **$21** of API usage on average to adapt a task, paid once per task
- **$5** for the render contract
- **$0.80** per further episode for simulation, rendering and review — no robot, no operator
- **$107** for one hour of three-view data, all in, versus a **$117** quote for teleoperation in China and **$290 in labour alone** in North America

## The Catch

One calibration episode is a real constraint. The agent is not learning the task from scratch; it is reconstructing a task it has already seen once. And the economics assume a video model that can render robot views photorealistically and cheaply, which is a moving target. The most valuable claim is not the dollar figure but the **87-versus-46 result**: the farm data is not merely cheaper, it is more robust to visual novelty than teleoperation, because the sim-to-real gap was never crossed in the first place.

Paper: [arXiv:2611.05320](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05320)
